speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege.
On March 6, 1964, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) tabled the Canada Year Book for the year 1963-64, in its English edition only, specifying that the French edition would be ready by June 1964, as we may see on page 619 of Hansard.
We are now in August, six months later, and we have not yet received the French edition of the Canada Year Book.
Further, we received the telephone book of the federal government and the House of Commons a month and a half ago in its English edition only. Six weeks later we have not yet received the French edition.
For the past two years we have asked for the French translation of Beauchesne's handbook of parliamentary procedure. On several occasions, we were told that it would soon be ready. But, there again, we have had no further news.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we notice that the French text of the standing and special committee reports are brought forward with still longer delays than it was formerly the case.
We believe that it is the privilege of all hon. members in the house to receive those volumes and material, which are most valuable for their work, in French as well as in English.
We have for some time noticed a certain neglect in this respect, and we are asking the government, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) to see to it that the translation services be improved so that we are treated on the same footing as the English speaking members and that our work is made as easy as theirs.
Mr. Speaker, we deemed it our duty to bring that situation to the attention of the
government because, at the time when we made vigorous representations, some effort was made to remedy the deficiency; but for several months, during which we were asked to give a chance to the one responsible for those productions, there seems to have been a slowing down and some carelessness in this respect.
In our opinion this matter is as important as it ever was before, even if we stopped recriminating the request of those in charge of that department.

speechtext:
1. In common with other individuals, corporations or financial institutions who borrow or lend, a chartered bank participates in the creation of new credit in the sense that its activities give rise to new financial assets and new financial liabilities. Like others who borrow (in the case of a chartered bank by taking deposits) the borrower must be ready to pay off its debts at maturity (which, in the case of the deposit liabilities of a chartered bank, is on demand or short notice); a chartered bank is dependent on public confidence in this respect for its continued existence.
Apart from conditions which must be met by any borrower, a chartered bank is required by the Bank Act to maintain a reserve in the form of "cash" (i.e. Bank of Canada notes and/or deposits with the Bank of Canada) equal on the average during each calendar month to not less than 8 per cent of its Canadian dollar deposits. By agreement with the Bank of Canada each chartered bank also holds a secondary reserve equal to at least 7 per cent of its Canadian dollar deposits, in government of Canada treasury bills and day-to-day loans to money market dealers. In addition to these reserves each chartered bank maintains substantial holdings of other short term government of Canada securities in order to assure its ability to meet any withdrawals by its depositors.
The total amount of "cash" reserves available to the chartered banks as a group is determined by the Bank of Canada in a manner consistent with its general objectives in the field of monetary policy and credit conditions. Given the public confidence referred to at the end of the first paragraph, the chartered banks as a group are able to acquire assets from the public in exchange for increased deposit liabilities in proportion to the volume of the "cash" reserves as made available by the central bank.

From the date of commencement of operations of the Bank of Canada on March 11, 1935, each chartered bank was limited in the issue of its own currency to an amount not in excess of the amount of its unimpaired paid-up capital and this maximum was reduced on the first day of January in each year for a period of five years commencing on January 1, 1936 by 5 per cent and on the first day of January in each year for a period of five years commencing on January 1, 1941 by 10 per cent. On January 1, 1950, each chartered bank was required to pay to the Bank of Canada an amount equal to the face value of its notes intended for circulation in Canada outstanding on that date and upon payment by each bank, the Bank of Canada became liable for the redemption of the notes issued by each bank. From that date the Bank of Canada has had the sole right to issue notes payable to bearer on demand and intended for circulation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, within the limitations that would necessarily be imposed I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he can give the house something of the picture of the situation in North Viet Nam. Realizing the awesome responsibility that rests on the United States to
Inquiries of the Ministry preserve the peace, what is the present position of affairs; and can he tell us whether any action has been taken to have this matter brought before the United Nations, it being apparently an unprovoked attack by the communists in an area 65 miles from the shore, which was completely inexcuseable on their part?

subsubtopic: U.S. POLICY FOLLOWING NAVAL ATTACKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house, of course, is aware of the statement made by the President and secretary of defense of the United States. Last night the Prime Minister of Canada received word from the secretary of state on behalf of the President that there had been another attack on United States ships in the gulf of Tonkin, and that it was his intention to order United States forces to take action to deter further attacks and so restrict the scale of military activity. As I said a moment ago, the President shortly thereafter spoke to the American people. I think I should draw the attention of the house to a very important passage in his statement, which is as follows:
Our response, for the present, will be limited and fitting. We Americans know, although others appear to forget, the risk of spreading conflict-we still seek no wider war.
There are two important ideas in this passage. The first is that the United States reaction is not to be widespread or excessive, but limited to what is considered necessary to deter a continuation of North Vietnamese attacks. The second is the assurance, which I am sure we all welcome, that the United States does not seek wider conflict. Furthermore, I believe we will all welcome the decision of the government of the United States to take this matter to the security council of the United Nations. There will be a meeting of that body this afternoon. It is to be hoped this will prevent the spread of hostilities. It will be understood why it is not possible to go further at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has not been consultation between the two governments in respect of the incidents of last evening. The secretary of state informed me of what had happened and of the action proposed to be taken by the government of the United States. It was, I think, quite appropriate that this should be done because Canada, after all, is a member of the international commission in Indochina. But I would not call this consultation. Other governments were, I believe, also informed in advance. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the action taken by the United States was a reaction to an attack made on United States ships on the high seas.

subsubtopic: U.S. POLICY FOLLOWING NAVAL ATTACKS

speechtext: Could I ask the Prime Minister if the Canadian government is prepared to make it clear that while we will support any action for the preservation of peace through the United Nations, we are not prepared to support military actions or attacks on naval bases which are carried on in support of discredited regimes and in order to buttress sawdust Caesars who are perpetuating dictatorships without the consent of their subjects?

subsubtopic: U.S. POLICY FOLLOWING NAVAL ATTACKS

subsubtopic: U.S. POLICY FOLLOWING NAVAL ATTACKS

speechtext:
I quite agree that the United States forces in the area are entitled to defend themselves against attack, and I am sure there is no disagreement in the house on that matter. I would point out also that it is desirable, as the President of the United States confirmed last night, that any reaction to an action taken against the United States should be limited to the requirements of the situation. We have already pointed out more


than once our views in this connection. I am quite sure that the United States government would limit-as they would desire to limit-their action in this matter to the requirements of the situation and to meeting an attack on their forces, in this case by a communist dictatorship in North Viet Nam.
I would also point out that if the countries in the area concerned lived up to their obligations under the Geneva accord we might not be in this serious situation.

speechtext: When we adjourned last evening the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned last night I was saying that when we assumed office in 1957 we inherited a dwindling economy and we endeavoured, during the years we managed the business of this country, to put that economy back on its feet, in keeping with the commitments we had made during the election campaigns.
We did so well that in 1963, when we were replaced by the present government, we left them an expanding economy. Indeed, we had passed measures which are still bearing fruit even today.
For instance, in the last election campaign we were criticized for having devaluated the Canadian dollar to 92 cents. Well, that is what enabled the Canadian economy to rise again.
I do not intend to speak at any great length this afternoon since the official opposition saw its positive efforts crowned with success these last few days.

We plied the minister with questions asking what were their plans concerning the expenditures they asked the house to vote.
After numerous repetitions and a great deal of pressure, we finally convinced certain ministers to give the required answers. But other answers must still be given. There are still one or two ministers to whom questions were put and who will surely take this opportunity to supply the information which is absolutely necessary to the good administration of public business.
I should not want to deprive my hon. friends of the pleasure and of the opportunity to perform their duty and, in concluding, I shall simply ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) to yield to the pressing and repeated requests made to him by the official opposition to cancel the 11 per cent tax which is disastrous for the Canadian people.
I should also like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) to take a look at the problem of eastern agriculture. It is well known that eastern agriculture is in a slump. Since this government took office we have been waiting for legislation designed to assist eastern farmers.
I should also like to urge the Minister of Industry and Defence Production (Mr. Drury) to take another look at his projects to set up as many jobs as possible. I take this opportunity to remind him that during the election the Liberal party promised the voters to provide 250,000 jobs each year. If we examine this last year's results, we notice that only 1,265 new jobs were created following the government's policy.
I warn the minister that this is not enough and that the Canadian people deserve more than 1,265 new jobs. They want action from the government.
Mr. Chairman, there are many other things I would like to say. I could talk at length about the quality of our industrial workers, particularly in the constituency I have the honour to represent here. But I would not want to deprive the ministers of the opportunity to justify their administration as heads of their respective departments and I stop to ask them, in particular the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh), to answer the numerous questions that have been asked.

I wish, sir, to make a somewhat extended reply to the hon. gentleman's observations; and since I imagine the reply will be mainly of interest to those who use the other official language of our country, which is not my mother tongue, I intend to make it in my version of their language.

In 1962, parliament authorized the Canadian government to appropriate approximately $16 million for the building of a railway between Matane and Ste. Anne des Monts, in the county of Gaspe.
After an extensive study of the question, the present government came to the conclusion that the construction of this railway line did not constitute at present the best possible use of the amounts ear-marked for transportation facilities so as to promote the economic development of the northern part of the Gaspe peninsula and that instead of building this line, it would be better to spend the amounts appropriated for that purpose on other projects more likely to meet the needs of that district with regard to transportation facilities.
Having consulted the province of Quebec and carried out a more thorough study, the government has come to the conclusion that the best contribution to transportation in the area would be to rebuild as early as possible the stretches of the north Gaspe highway which still do not meet modern standards. Of course, we realize that road building comes under the provinces, but we are told that there is such a backlog in Quebec's road building and rebuilding program that the Gaspe highway will not be completed before several years, unless special financial assistance is provided in that connection.
Since parliament had already recognized in principle the necessity for Ottawa to take steps to improve transport facilities in that area, the government has decided that, subject to parliament's approval, it will make a substantial contribution to the completion of the north Gaspe highway.
During our negotiations with the Quebec authorities we learned that some 87 miles had to be reconstructed in the constituencies of

The government has agreed to pay $125,000 per mile for the construction and profiling as well as $25,000 for the paving of those 87 miles for each mile completed before November 1, 1968 up to a maximum federal contribution of $13 million. The payments applicable to the completed work will be made at the end of each quarter, following an appropriate inspection made by the engineers of the trans-Canada highway division of the Department of Public Works.
The Quebec department of highways has agreed to undertake as soon as possible the work on every section of the road in both countries. The substitution of a road to the planned railroad as item of expenditure does not exclude for ever the possibility of a railroad being built. If the area develops to such an extent as to justify its construction, the project will of course be reconsidered.
There will be an item in the next supplementary estimates authorizing the contemplated expenditures.
It will be noted that the federal government does not intend to allocate the complete sum of $16 million to the road; we feel that part of this money could usefully serve for the development of airports and harbours which come under the direct jurisdiction of the federal government.
A number of plans for the development of harbours have been approved in principle and appropriate items will be entered in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Public Works.
The Department of Transport will also add an item in its supplementary estimates for the improvement of the Gaspe airport. This department has also undertaken a survey of the Gaspe peninsula in order to find an appropriate site for a district airport which would serve the main towns in the county of Gaspe.
The projects already approved will not take up all the moneys provided for the development of transport in the Gaspe peninsula, and other plans will be undertaken as the need arises.

Mr. Chairman, I compliment the minister on the way in which he speaks the French language and assure him that even those who only know English will,
I am sure, understand everything he says when he speaks in French. His pronunciation is of such a nature that even those who are not erudite in the language can certainly understand him.
I wonder if the right hon. gentleman would allow me to say I have been told the Manitoba accent is better than the Saskatchewan accent.

I would not like to enter into a comparison, because I thought the hon. gentleman had a Newfoundland accent. I am surprised he has suddenly disavowed that province and gone to the province of his origin. The chickens sometimes come home to roost.
This announcement by the minister is one that I find difficulty in understanding. I am not now speaking of the fact that the minister spoke in French, but of the content of his statement. I am surprised that a government which, according to its own protestations, has been so diligent in the preservation of provincial rights has suddenly departed from all those principles.
I point out that there is a statute of parliament making available $16 million for the building of a railroad to meet the needs of the people in the Gaspe peninsula, who for many years have been asking for it. I visited that area at length. I saw something of its needs, and according to the business people with whom I came in contact those needs could not be met in any other way than through a railroad to encourage development and to make transportation available for its mineral and lumber production.
This government come into office and what do they do? They simply state "We are not going to follow a statute of parliament; we are going to take another course. We have consulted with the government of Quebec and we have decided that the greatest contribution which could be made to the transportation facilities would be the reconstruction of those sections of the north Gaspe highway which are not at present built to modern standards.''
We recognized, of course, that the construction of highways was a provincial function, but we were told that the government of Quebec had such a backlog of construction and reconstruction that it would be several years before the Gasp6 highway could be completed-
This shows up the hypocrisy of the policies of this government. It speaks of provincial rights and then proceeds to build highways which come exclusively within the jurisdiction of the province.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure-
I did not interrupt the minister-

No, but I am sure the right hon. gentleman does not want to misrepresent the statement. The government has no intention whatever of building this highway. It only intends to make a financial contribution to it, as the right hon. gentleman's government did to many highways when he was in office.

Quite the reverse; and the loudness of the interruption betrays the depth of the guilt. This is a complete subterfuge. This is something that constitutes an invasion of the very basis of the constitutional rights of the provinces. The minister mentions assisting in the building of highways. We provided highway assistance for roads to resources in the various provinces, under agreement with the various provinces and with the provinces contributing their respective shares. That was quite a different thing from this. The statement says:
After consultation with the government of Quebec... the government decided that the greatest contribution which could be made to the transportation facilities of the region would be the speedy reconstruction of those sections of the north Gaspe highway which are not at present built to modem standards...
From our discussions with the Quebec authorities we learned that there were some 87 miles of highway No. 6 in Matane and north Gaspe counties which require reconstruction. The government has agreed to contribute $125,000 per mile toward the construction and grading and an additional $25,000 toward the paving of these 87 miles of road on every mile that is completed before November 1, 1968, with an upper limit of $13,000,000 on the federal contribution.
This is the complete antithesis of everything which this government has advocated throughout the years, and I ask the question, why? What business have they, as a government, without bringing an existing statute before parliament to be repealed, to say "We are not going to follow the statute. The law means nothing to us. We intend to evade the law by following a different course while expending the same amount of money".
Whatever the benefit may be-and I am not belittling the benefits which will follow from highway construction-this constitutes an affront to parliament. It constitutes on the part of the Liberal government a disregard of constitutional rights and a disregard for and contempt of parliament. I mention this, and I think other hon. members may deal therewith. What was asked for was a railway, and because of the sense of guilt felt by hon. gentlemen opposite, in office for so many years without doing anything for the Gaspe area, and because they did not want to carry out this policy which we had consummated

So I leave it to the government. Give us answers to the questions that have been placed before you. Get off your pedestal of silence that you sat on all last week and get down in the House of Commons to answering these questions. I repeat what I said earlier, that at no time has this been in the nature of a filibuster. I say that definitely and absolutely. It is all very well to try to explain the difference between the circumstances of today and those of 1962. But it is convenient today for the government to conceal its lack of action, its failure to meet economic problems, its denial of parliament to deal with such matters as the pension measure; it is convenient to say, "The reason we have not acted is that the opposition have prevented us from so doing". Nothing of the kind-it has been the failure on the part of the government.
Let me add something more. The pension legislation has been before the house three times; there was the first edition, the withdrawn edition; the revised edition, and then the present edition. I think we would be doing a worth-while job if this edition were brought before the house now, before we adjourned, because this is a matter that deserves the immediate consideration of the house. Let them bring it forward now and we will be able to do our part to expedite it; because, as I have said on more than one occasion, we do not intend to swallow the bait of a promise of a recess for giving up our responsibilities. We do not place recess ahead of responsibility.
Now, sir, I mention one other matter because the Minister of Transport today brought before the house the question of the speech delivered outside the house by the Secretary of State with regard to federal assistance being provided through a loan fund to the movie industry. We knew this in anticipation,

because the minister when speaking at the Couchiching conference dealt with this matter in general. I am not going into detail at this time, but let me say this: At a time when there are so many problems facing Canada, does it seem that this is a matter of priority? Should the Canadian government assume some of the risks of private film production? I question that seriously. What cultural development, to which lip service is given in the statement of the minister, can be achieved in this way? And what is to be the result? Is parliament to be placed in the position of bonusing a private industry in order that it may increase its profits? These are questions that will be asked. Is the national film board-and it has done a good job in its field-to be the agent of the government in its attempt to compete with Hollywood or with the British movie industry? Canada certainly is not ignored now by the movie industry. Many movies are made in Canadian settings with Canadian actors and Canadian technicians, and I refer to films like "Mr. Pearson".
These are questions that are asked. Is it the government's intention to have movies made for Canadians or to have movies made to show Canada to other people? In either case a question will arise as to whether the cultural growth in Canada will be manifestly increased. And I would not want to inject anything of a partisan nature into this discussion, but would not the C.B.C. with its waste of money on the film "Mr. Pearson" be emulated by the national film board? I ask that question, not expecting an answer to it today.
I hope that the ministers will pursue the laudable course that they have in the last 24 hours and will give an answer to the various questions, so that together in cooperation we will be able to achieve that which we set out to do, namely to carry out an examination in those fields in respect of which parliament has had no information. Our responsibility according to every constitutional work has been carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I think that I should be allowed to exercise my right under the rules to take exception, and I am going to do so as objectively and as non controversially as possible, to one or two statements made by the right hon. gentleman relating to the announcement I made this afternoon about assistance to the North Gasp6 highway.
I should like first to remind the right hon. gentleman that parliament did not ap-

propriate any money whatsoever for the railway. All it did was permit the government, if it saw fit, to have the C.N.R. spend up to $16 million for the road. When we came into office it was our duty, as it was the duty of the previous government, to decide in each case whether the crown should recommend a particular expenditure to parliament. We gave this very careful consideration, and it is now months since we told the house that we did not think this was the best way to use that money. That seems to dispose of any question of contempt of parliament, because parliament did not order the government to build the road, but merely said that if moneys were appropriated for the railway it could be built. We know that no railway more than three miles long can be built without the consent of parliament. Parliament cannot, through one of these bills, and did not in this case, appropriate the money. I think that deals with the constitutional point.
As for the announcement I made today in respect of assistance in building this highway, I should like to state that this is precisely the same kind of assistance provided under the roads to resources program and the trans-Canada highway program.
No.
An agreement has been made with the government of the province, and the hon. gentleman himself read the word "agreed".
I was reading from the hon. gentleman's statement.

You were reading from my statement, but the right hon. gentleman did read the word "agreed".
There has been an exchange of letters between the provincial minister of highways, after consultation with the government of the province, and myself as Minister of Transport, after consultation with our government, and we have agreed that we will contribute a certain amount of money on a per mile basis toward the construction of the road, when the province has built it and it has been properly inspected. This assistance is exactly on all fours with the kind of assistance provided in the past.
No, not at all.

There is no question whatsoever of our building the road or of our doing anything except making a grant to the province, if parliament approves, similar to grants that were made in respect of the roads to

resources program and the trans-Canada highway project.
This is quite different.

Of course the right hon. gentleman makes assertions, but assertions do not make facts. These are the facts. The facts are within my knowledge. No amount of assertion by the right hon. gentleman will alter the facts.
I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. Apparently this is a joint program. I thought joint programs were completely taboo in the thinking of the present government.

Actually, if the right hon. gentleman would listen occasionally and read occasionally, instead of constantly thinking of what he is going to say next and how he can change the sense of what someone else has said, he would keep out of a lot of the difficulty he gets into and end a lot of the confusion for which he must accept responsibility. Of course I could not do this kind of thing because I am a simple straightforward fellow.
Oh, oh.

I will not say I admire this, because it is not something I particularly admire, but one cannot help admire art even though one does not like it. I do not think there is a man in this country, not even the hon. member for Port Arthur, who can make black look as much like white or white to look as much like black as can the right hon. member for Prince Albert. Still, when he has completed his verbal painting, black is still black and white is still white.
This government has never at any time anywhere said that we were opposed to joint programs. We have said that we were prepared in certain circumstances to have a province contract out of joint programs, and that is the position.
This program in fact is not a joint program but a contribution to a provincial function, just as was the assistance provided to the trans-Canada highway, which was not a joint program. Surely a joint program is something that is undertaken jointly. When one makes a specific and definite contribution surely all one is doing is making an earmarked grant, and that is not a joint program. As I conceive a joint program, it is something that is done in common by two governments. This project is not going to be carried out in common by two governments. The work will be done entirely by the prointerim Supply
vincial department of highways, and when it has been done to certain standards payments will be made, provided parliament sees fit to grant the money for the making of the payments. Mr. Chairman, I felt that I should make this point clear immediately after the right hon. gentleman's statement.
I do not know whether the committee will also permit me to answer the questions asked by the right hon. gentleman in respect of the feature film industry, but I think the best way to answer those questions is to read the statement that my colleague, the Secretary of State, is going to make elsewhere. If that is agreeable I will do so, and I suppose I have the right to speak in this committee in any event.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the hon. gentleman.

Yes. Before the minister proceeds with another subject will he permit me to ask a question?
Certainly.

If the C.N.R., or the Ontario Northland Railway in northern Ontario wished to build a branch line would the Minister of Transport agree to a joint program or an earmarked grant in respect of that line, just as has been done in respect of the north Gaspe road?

Mr. Chairman, you will appreciate that there is a very salutary rule that all governments ignore at their peril, and all politicians ignore at their peril, and that is the rule which says one should not answer hypothetical questions. I have not the slightest intention of attempting to answer the question. If the Ontario Northland Railway does decide at some time to build a railway I am sure the government will give consideration to any proposal from Ontario. I am sure the government, no matter what government it was, would give careful consideration to any proposal from the government of Ontario and would not say no in advance; but that does not in the least mean they would say yes.
For 22 years you did nothing.
The hon. gentleman was there for six years and all he did was get a permissive statute on the books-

Then you wiped it out.

-and having done that he lost the seat.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit a question that is not hypothetical? Would he not agree that the formula he has outlined is identical with the formula that was used in connection with the roads to resources program, and that program was regarded as a joint program?

I am not sure that it is. As a matter of fact, I did not know it was but I dare say the hon. gentleman is right. I never administered the roads to resources program and the hon. gentleman did. If he says that was a joint program I would assume this is a joint program in the same sense that was. I do not see anything wrong with it at all, or with any other joint program which is properly based and with which both governments agree. But it is another matter to try, within provincial jurisdiction, to impose policies on provincial governments, and we do not believe in that. But there is no imposition here at all. There is complete agreement about the desirability of doing this on the part of both governments.
While we are on that subject may I ask a question? If the minister says this is a joint program between the province of Quebec and the federal government, what is the proportion of payment?

The province is going to build the road, whatever it costs, and we are going to make a specific contribution of $125,000 a mile when it is graded and another $25,000 a mile when it is paved. What the proportions will be will not be determined until the road is built. It will depend on how much it costs, but since the open-ended part is entirely provincial that is no concern of ours.
Open at both ends.

It is only open at the provincial end. Our end is completely closed and it is closed twice. There is a ceiling of $13 million and there is a payment of $125,000 a mile for grading and $25,000 a mile for paving. All the rest of the cost, whatever it may be, will be borne by the provincial government. Therefore that is not a matter of concern to us as members of the parliament of Canada. It is a matter of concern to the residents, the legislators and the government of Quebec.

May I address a question to the minister? Why did the minister ignore

the petition addressed to him by the chamber of commerce of Gaspe north, including the former Liberal member, requesting federal construction of the road in Gaspe?
I think the hon. member for Gaspe will give a better reply to that than I will, but I can say that the petition was not ignored. It was very carefully considered.
It was ignored.

If the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm has finished his act I will now turn to films. The statement I am now going to read is a statement that the Secretary of State is making this afternoon with regard to the film board.

I wonder whether the minister would leave out the padding and just refer to the material parts. It is all very interesting to say that we have become one of the richest countries of the world and that our standard of living is second only to the United States and Sweden. These things are interesting matters of information but we want to know about the film board itself.
I always understood that the right hon. gentleman was a great exponent of freedom of speech-
Go on.

-and I am sure he would not want to censor my speeches in advance of my making them, particularly when they are not mine. I am merely going to give the committee the speech that is being made elsewhere by the Secretary of State. Although I can understand the right hon. gentleman wanting to have it altered a bit, I think it would be better to give it as my colleague proposes to give it.

Apparently the hon.
gentleman has not read it.

The right hon. gentleman can talk about that when he is on a level with all the rest of us, after all of us have heard it and not just those who appear to have had a preview.
While not detracting in any way from the important contribution which the film board has made to Canadian life both at home and abroad, we cannot be equally happy about the present state of the Canadian film industry in all its aspects. Unlike most other countries with similar problems and similar professional talents, we seem to have been unable to bring forth a film industry in Canada which could find its inspiration in a Canadian setting and produce and distribute a Canadian made product to place alongside the production of the national film board.

If I may interpose something, the right hon. gentleman will see that it is not proposed to have these feature films made by the film board but by the film industry.
There is nothing new about this problem and clearly it was intended that one of the functions of the board would be to assist through its own activities in the development of a Canadian film industry. This surely the board must continue to do.
In recent months, the government has become particularly interested in this vital Canadian aspect of our national life. We have come to the conclusion that the establishment of a feature film industry in Canada is highly desirable and that technical facilities and talent are available in our country to make such a development practicable. We are also conscious of the fact that some form of public financial assistance is required to foster the Canadian feature film Industry.
Therefore it is the intention of the government to ask parliament for the necessary authority to establish a loan fund for the production of feature films of high quality in Canada. In our view, one of the important limiting factors in our country has been the availability of risk capital to finance such film production.
It will take some months before the authority can be secured from parliament to undertake this program. The government, with the assistance of the national film board and in consultation with the industry, intends to use this period for a further intensive study of the problems faced by the feature film industry, including the distribution problem both at home and abroad. A more detailed announcement of government plans will be made when these studies have been completed.
I believe that the feature length film industry which we hope will see the light of day, and develop, will benefit from the creative impulse the national film board has been giving for the past 25 years. I sincerely hope that, through the joint efforts of both the private producers and the board, Canadians in the near future will appear more and more frequently on screens at home and abroad, either in feature length or short films. This will be a new sign of our growing cultural maturity.
I think that answers most of the questions that were asked by the right hon. gentleman. It makes it quite clear that this loan fund is not designed or intended to be available to the film board but to the private film industry. We have a private film industry in Canada. For example, one might mention Crawley Films located here in Ottawa. That firm has done some very good work in short films. But there has not yet been a successful feature film industry. If one can be developed by way of loans, this will contribute to employment for a number of Canadians who now have to look for employment in some other country. To the extent that it is successful it will tend to help somewhat in our balance of payments problem. It will have a number of advantages of a material and practical nature apart altogether from any cultural advantages it may have. I have a certain responsibility in connection with
Interim Supply
this matter because I was the secretary of state when we first began to study the project. I authorized the study, and it has come to fruition under my colleague, the present Secretary of State. I therefore feel a certain responsibility for joining in this recommendation.
I feel there are enough prospects for success that it is worth while to try and get a Canadian feature film industry, not a government film industry but a film industry by private companies. If a government loan fund will accomplish this, it will be a good thing. I believe it is true that no country in the world, except the United States, has been able to develop a feature film industry without some kind of governmental support. The British film industry has always had it and so, I have been given to understand, have the film industries of every other country except the United States which produces films. Some of them have the natural advantage of linguistic protection which we do not have in Canada, and which the British do not have, against the United States industry.
As to whether or not any of this loan will be used to make a feature film about the Prime Minister or even the right hon. gentleman, I cannot say, although I believe they would both be wonderful subjects for a feature film. All I hope is that if such a film is undertaken, it is undertaken by private industry in an exclusively private way.

I rise merely for the purpose of clarifying the situation with regard to the Matane and St. Anne des Monts railway. The minister generally has the answers to all questions on matters that come within his department, and he spoke with the authority that he does. When he speaks loudly, he speaks with less authority, and in this case he spoke very loudly. He indicated there had been no fixed amount voted by parliament-
I did not say that.
Yes, you did.
I said no money had been appropriated.

I am going to read the statute in order to establish the facts. I am quoting from chapter 13 of the statutes for 1962:
In order to establish railway services between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts, in the province of Quebec, and otherwise to assist in the development of the Gaspe peninsula, the governor in council may provide for the appointment of Canadian National Railway Company. ..as agent of Her Majesty for the construction and completion, prior to the 31st day of December, 1964, or such later

Interim Supply
date as the governor in council may fix, of the line of railway.. .described in the schedule-
I am leaving out the unnecessary words.
Estimates of the mileage of the railway line, the amount to be expended on the construction thereof and the average expenditure per mile are set out in the schedule, and, except with the approval of the governor in council, such estimates shall not be exceeded by more than fifteen per cent.
The governor in council shall pay to the company an amount equal to the cost to the company of constructing the railway line, including the cost of survey of location.. .but not exceeding in any case the sum of sixteen million, one hundred thousand dollars.
That is definite and complete; no appropriation by parliament is required. We passed this act and the minister is thoroughly wrong and completely inconsistent in what he says. He has not read this act, you see. Section 4 of the act reads:
The amount of the payment hereby authorized shall be paid to the company out of the consolidated revenue fund by the payment, from time to time, at the direction of the governor in council upon the report of the Minister of Transport as to the mileage of railway line constructed or to be constructed, of such amounts, in such manner and subject to such conditions, if any, as the governor in council deems expedient.
In other words, we do appropriate in parliament, from the consolidated revenue fund, an amount not to exceed $16,100,000. The railway was to be completed by December 31, 1964, unless the governor in council for some reason extended the period. This is what parliament said.
Finally the schedule sets out that the mileage shall be approximately 57 miles, the cost of construction $14 million and the average cost per mile, $245,614. I repeat what it said. You just have to read the statute to appreciate fully the fact that this government has treated contemptuously a statute of parliament and refused to carry it out.

In so far as the point of order is concerned, Mr. Chairman, surely this committee cannot accept the statement just made by the leader of the Creditiste party. Mr. Chairman, I thank you for the wise ruling you have just made, and I merely wish to point out to the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary that nobody ever said that we had been deprived of our rights. It was only suggested that Conservative members have spoken for so long and so often that it would be reasonable to give the floor to a member of another party from time to time. It was never suggested that the chairman had shown discrimination against members of other parties. That is not true at all.
We admit that we simply did not rise because we did not want to indulge in filibustering, and if I am taking part in the debate at present, it is because the Leader of the Opposition saw fit to speak at this time, when the leaders of the opposition parties have been called to the Prime Minister's office.
And also because he commented on the statement of the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) with regard to the railway project between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts.
Mr. Chairman, I am not representing that area, but I know it rather well, because I go there every year. Moreover, I have been interested in the matter for a long time. When the Leader of the Opposition stated that some requests had been made for the construction of that railroad section, I think that he was perhaps expressing ideas which took shape in the mind of various politicians, Liberal as well as Conservative.

Indeed, the idea of building a railroad between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts was initiated entirely by politicians about 20 years ago, when they wanted to get votes in the county of Gaspe, by promising the people a railway, and more particularly telling them that this project would solve all their economic problems. Now, after having heard such a statement for the last 20 years or so, the people of Gaspe finally believed that this railway would really solve the problems they had to face.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the building of a railway at this time would in no way help the economic development of the Gaspe area, and that is why I am theoretically satisfied with the solution put forward by the government, the more so as there seems to have been some agreement with the government authorities of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, as I said before, I am basically opposed to some agreements and some joint plans. Yet, the government of the province being the representative of that province, I think that we should accept the agreements concluded between the representatives of a province and the federal government.
Moreover, when referring to the statement made by the Minister of Transport on July 18 last in connection with the Atlantic development board and super highways in the maritimes, it is realized that the federal government will pay a grant of $3 million to every Atlantic province to enable them to develop their existing roads or to construct sections which have not been completed. Consequently, since the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote) has already asked that the Gaspe peninsula be included in the Atlantic area, I feel that the Gaspe peninsula should take advantage of the grants given by the federal government. In fact, we know that the Gaspe peninsula has been neglected for a long time and that it still is by the provincial as well as the federal governments. But at last, it seems that an attempt is being made to help the people of that area, and I feel that the idea set forth today by the Minister of Transport should be accepted.
Personally, I believe that those $13 million could be more adequately spent, that it could more realistically create full employment, if this government was willing, for example, to contribute to the establishment of five industries worth some $2.5 million each in the Gaspe peninsula. This would definitely help the people of the Gaspe peninsula not only

to build or improve a road which would only create temporary jobs, but would also contribute to assure more or less permanent employment. I suggest that such a procedure would be more adequate and would more easily solve the problems of the Gaspe district. -the report on that survey has not been received yet.

member has bravely enunciated his opinion concerning the construction of the railway line between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts, could he tell the house if he is still in favour, as a possible substitute, of the deepening of the Matapedia river?

Mr. Chairman, when we talk about the Matane-Ste Anne des Monts area, we know that it really needs to be developed.
As I said earlier, building a road or improving it might be helpful for a while.

I am not talking about Matane. I know that Matane has been greatly favoured, the same as almost all the areas outside Gasp6 itself.

I think that, if an election is forthcoming, the Liberal party should be in a position, within a few weeks, to carry out achievements which will no longer be mere election promises but something of value to the people of Gaspe.
They have a knack for that.
For achievements, yes.

I am glad to see that that region, which suffered so much from the fact that "patronage" was being carried out elsewhere, will benefit at last from some patronage. At least, that should help it to get out of its financial slump.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to go any further. As 1 said a while ago, I had no intention whatever of indulging in obstruction. I merely wished to express certain views concerning the statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).

Mr. Chairman, the statement made to the committee by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) will be welcomed by the people of Gaspe, in particular by the development board of eastern Quebec.
The projects announced for the Gaspe peninsula, particularly the reconstruction of highway No. 6, show in a tangible way that the Ottawa and Quebec governments are interested in the growth of under developed areas.
Tremendous development efforts based on serious studies and effective participation by the people are under way in the Gaspe peninsula. The governments concerned are duty bound to support the efforts of the people to find a solution to their problems.
Those tangible works will help to prove that the governments intend to take seriously the efforts made by the population. Those undertakings must, therefore, be seen in that light.
In a few days the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) will announce officially a project that has been under consideration for many years and which will be of a great assistance in the Gaspe south development. Later on.

A few minutes ago the Leader of the Opposition had in his hand an extract of the legislation which received royal assent on March 23, 1962, that is chapter 13, 10-11 Elizabeth II.
I should now like to summarize what happened. The bill which was given royal assent on March 23, 1962, authorized the construction of 57 miles of railroad at an estimated cost of $16,100,000. Order in council 1962-481 dealt in a little more detail with the agreement which was to be signed between the government and the C.N.R. That order in council was approved on April 5, 1962, but the most interesting item in all that is order in council PC-656 of May 1962.
The first paragraph read as follows:

His Excellency the Governor General In council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Transport, pursuant to section 4 of chapter 13, Statutes of Canada, 1962, is pleased hereby to direct as follows:-
1.	That an accountable payment, in the amount of $100,000 be made to the Canadian National Railway Company out of the consolidated revenue fund to provide funds to cover the estimated cost of the work of construction of the line of railway between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts in the province of Quebec, during the period April 16 1962 to June 30, 1962.

The Leader of the Opposition, who was then prime minister, said nothing about that. There were elections on April 8, and we know what change this meant for the whole of Canada.

Your railway, you will have it. said the Prime Minister to the people attending the meeting, last nighb-

And the Leader of the Opposition comes and tells the house that everything was ready to go ahead with that project.
Mr. Chairman, when statistics show that for the nine counties of lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe as a whole annual production is valued at $85 million and social security payments at $110 million, it is high time that our leaders work together toward the elimination of that gap between production and social security payments of all sorts.

The policy of federal contribution to the provincial road system is being carried out in the maritime provinces, as mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency (Mr. Marcoux), but, in the maritimes, this contribution has to go through the Atlantic development board; however, is it not a fact that the Gaspe peninsula suffers from a similar, if not worse, economic stagnation than some of the Atlantic regions?
Once the Gaspe peninsula is provided with good seaports, good airports and improved highways, it will be possible to develop more rationally its natural resources.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, everyone notices that the session is going on and on and on, and that nothing or almost nothing is being done. At long last the ministers decided to answer questions yesterday. Before that, for a week or almost ten days, questions were not being answered.
Do you know, Mr. Chairman, the impression thus created among the general public, among those people we see here in the galleries this afternoon and especially among those who are not here, but all across Canada? They are under the impression that the House of Commons is a place where members behave like school kids and play a game of asking questions concerning the flag and the estimates, blaming the government for not answering questions, and that the government is in no hurry to assume its responsibilities. So, the present situation is that among the public, we are considered as people who waste public funds and moneys paid by the people in the form of taxes.
A while ago I heard the Leader of the Opposition say that 250 questions had remained without reply and that only since yesterday had the ministers decided to answer in a proper way the questions asked by the opposition during the last week.
Two Conservative hon. members observed a few minutes ago that they did not wish to conduct a filibuster but that we, on this side, perhaps did not want to assume our responsibilities.
That is not the issue at all but I could say to the Conservatives and to those who rose a while ago, that their filibuster has been systematic since last week and that, concerning the questions for which answers are being requested now, when they were in power, a little over a year ago, the same questions remained without reply and that the government, and the then prime minister, who is now Leader of the Opposition, did not even take the trouble to answer the questions we

asked at that time. And now they accuse others of not doing what they themselves neglected to do when they were in office.
We have also read in the newspapers this morning that there was a meeting of the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition yesterday for 25 minutes in order to try and find a compromise. Later this afternoon there will be a meeting of leaders of all parties in the house. But what I do not quite understand and can hardly imagine is that the Leader of the Opposition, alone with the Prime Minister, decides on some sort of a compromise, and it is then that the ministers started answering or appeared willing to answer questions asked by the opposition.
That there are efforts, Mr. Chairman, to leave aside the other members of the house- I intended to say this at noon when the Prime Minister was here-is incomprehensible. We in this corner of the house were elected exactly the same way as the Prime Minister of Canada and the Leader of the Opposition. As far as I am concerned, I even got a much larger majority than the Prime Minister in his riding and the Leader of the Opposition in his.
We do not like little meetings to which the leaders of the other political groups in the house are not invited. I find this wrong and illogical. The Leader of the Opposition has no rights to talk with the Prime Minister in the name of the opposition, because he is not alone in the opposition; we also are in the opposition and we should be entitled to take part in the discussions, if there are agreements to be reached with respect to the ausiness of the house.
Besides, we shall see later when we get together how far we can co-operate.
We have been offering our co-operation concerning the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag for a long time. Three weeks ago, perhaps a little less, I said that all the Creditistes members were ready to vote in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag, no matter which flag it was, whether it has one, three or even 12 maple leaves. You can add as many leaves as you want. But as far as a distinctive Canadian flag is concerned, we are all ready to vote in favour of such a flag.
Would the hon. member allow me a simple question?
By all means.

Is the hon. member in favour of two official flags resolutions, including the

union jack? Does not the hon. member find that ridiculous?

I was under the impression that my hon. friend for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm was quicker in the uptake.
We have before us a resolution in two parts: part A which we are now discussing and part B which will be discussed later. On part A, we are unanimous-
So am I.

I understand that the hon. member also agrees with us.
On part B, we will be unanimous; that is to vote against a second flag for Canada. Is that clear enough?

gentleman rising on a question of privilege or a point of order?

Among the 1,647 questions that were asked since the beginning of this session, 1,530, that is 92.9 per cent were answered, whereas only 118, that is 7.1 per cent, were not.

And here is the answer:
Butter-33 cents per lb. Canadian seaboard.

sold butter-I have a whole list of them here, including Toronto, Quebec, Montreal, Winnipeg, Ottawa. This was the answer:

Mr. Chairman, I should now like to deal with a question asked by my good friend, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) relating to the banking system. It is question No. 1,302 which was as follows:
1. Do the chartered banks create new credits and, if so (a) in what way (b) must they furnish sureties (c) what are those sureties (d) in what proportion?
Mr. Chairman, listen to this answer. You can realize how clear it is.
1. In common with other individuals, corporations or financial institutions who borrow or lend, a chartered bank participates in the creation of new credit-
That is what the official is stating in his answer.
In common with other individuals, corporations or financial institutions who borrow or lend, a chartered bank participates in the creation of new credit-
And this, although it is formally established that only chartered banks have the right to create new credit, that no one, no financial institution enjoys that privilege, and that the companies that borrow or lend must use new credit created by chartered banks to continue their operations.
But now an official of the Department of Finance in Ottawa, because he does not know, is stating in his answer that the banks are only doing like other lending corporations. In fact, here is what he said:
Like others who borrow-in the case of a chartered bank by taking deposits-the borrower must be ready to pay off its debt at maturity-
Mr. Chairman, there is no need for an official to tell us that. We know it. And I continue:
-the borrower must be ready to pay off his debt at maturity (which, in the case of the deposit liabilities of a chartered bank, is on demand or

Interim Supply
short notice) a chartered bank is dependent on public confidence in this respect for its continued existence.
Mr. Chairman, we agree on that point. And I go on:
Apart from conditions which must be met by any borrower, a chartered bank is required by the Bank Act to maintain a reserve in the form of cash (i.e. Bank of Canada notes and/or deposits with the Bank of Canada) equal on the average during each calendar year to not less than 8 per cent of its Canadian dollar deposits. By agreement with the Bank of Canada, each chartered bank also holds a secondary reserve, equal to at least 7 per cent of its Canadian dollar deposits, in government of Canada treasury bills and day-to-day loans to money market dealers. In addition to these reserves, each chartered bank maintains substantial holdings of other short term government of Canada securities in order to assure its ability to meet any withdrawals by its depositors.
Mr. Chairman, the chartered banks have enjoyed for a long time the federal government guarantee under the Bank Act. In fact, they have the right to multiply by 12 their deposits with the Bank of Canada. It is against this control that we fight and that we fought in the past.
Moreover, we do not like officials to answer with so little clearness the questions we ask, and I feel that lectures in political economy should be given them by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay), who is an economist, by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne), who is also an economist, or by people who must have a knowledge of financial and monetary questions. Let those people give lectures to the officials of the Department of Finance so that they will not answer us by nonsense such as we find in the answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Roberval.
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take more of the time of the house, because I think that we will discuss tomorrow the meeting which will be held later with leaders of the other political parties. But before I resume my seat, I want to repeat that the leader of the official opposition must not consider himself as the leader of all opposition parties.
The Liberals are accused of arrogance, but the leader of the official opposition acts in an arrogant way with the other members of the opposition. If he leads a more important group or a greater number of members, I feel that I lead more Quebec members than he, and that Raillement Creditiste has the right to be heard as often and as freely as any member of the official opposition.
Mr. Chairman, we shall go and see which understanding it is possible to reach, because we also want the end of the session. As I
[Mr. Caouette.l
said at the beginning of my remarks, it seems that the public are tired of seeing the members of parliament act like school children, and the teachers of these school children seem obviously to be the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition. Let us stop acting like children and let us pass legislative measures likely to help the Canadian people, instead of aggravating them as we do now.

Mr. Chairman, just a few remarks to answer the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette).
For the information of the hon. member, I must say that all members of the official opposition are completely free to express their views, according to their feelings, and the leader of the official opposition has never taken me to task because of a statement I had made in the house, regarding the flag issue or any other matter. I am extremely pleased to be a member of the Conservative party, to be a member of the official opposition, for I have always enjoyed the fullest freedom in expressing my opinions, according to my feelings, without any other members intervening or exerting influence in order to prevent me from expressing my opinions.
Mr. Chairman, we have always been prepared to co-operate with the government to expedite the passing of interim supply bills. We wanted to co-operate. We have asked many questions concerning eastern agriculture which is now in a state of stagnation, since eastern farmers, especially Quebec farmers, are going bankrupt.
According to what I have learned from reliable sources, the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) will be absent from this country for a month. He is on holidays and will not be back until the end of August.
Mr. Chairman, even if the Minister of Forestry is gone, even if, although we wished to co-operate with the government, we did get all the answers to the questions we asked-and it is the role of the opposition to put questions to the government when expenditures of $700 million are at stake- even if we did not obtain full co-operation, I can assure the government, on behalf of the official opposition, that we shall vote interim supply before six o'clock this evening. Indeed, I shall be the last speaker on this side of the house.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to deal with the statements made following the statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), and with the speech made by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr). The latter stated

that it would be foolish to build the Mata-pedia-Matane railway. In my opinion he is wrong. I know that several hon. members have received a letter from the chamber of commerce of Gaspe north and an extract from the minutes of the meeting of the board of directors of this chamber of commerce, following its last meeting.
I received this letter, dated June 22, 1964, and I wish to quote the following:
Extract from the minutes of the board of directors meeting at Ste Anne des Monts, on Wednesday, June 17, 1964.
The chamber of commerce of Gaspe North Inc. wishes to get the record straight regarding an article recently published in the newspapers, including he Soleil, in which it was stated that the chamber of commerce of Gaspe North Inc., had definitely given up the project regarding the building of a railway between Matane and Ste Anne des Monts.
The board of directors of the chamber of commerce of Gaspe North has never taken such a stand and the question of its giving up this project never came up. Quite on the contrary, the chamber continues to support that project and it is convinced of the necessity of building that railway for the development of the area. The house supports road and harbour construction projects without giving up the railway project. Roads and harbours are necessary with or without a railway.
Moreover, it was proposed by Claude Jourdain-
Mr. Chairman, at this stage, may I be permitted to point out that Mr. Claude Jourdain is the former Liberal member for Gaspe in the Quebec legislature. I continue:
-seconded by Maurice Lefrancois and unanimously carried that the chamber of commerce of North Gaspe Inc. ask the federal government to extend by at least a year the date of expiry of the bill, set at present for December 31, 1964.
That a copy of that statement and resolution be addressed to the Minister of Transport, the Prime Minister of Canada, Hon. Rene Tremblay, Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, Mr. Alexandre Cyr, member for Gaspe, the newspaper he Soleil, the newspaper he Voyageur and the regional chamber of commerce of Gaspe.
Mr. Chairman, I have read with interest the statement made by the Minister of Transport in which he says among other things the following:
The government has agreed to contribute $125,000 per mile towards the construction and grading and an additional $25,000 towards the paving of these 87 miles of road on every mile that is completed before November 1, 1968, with an upper limit of $13,000,000 on the federal contribution.
The amounts relating to the finished work will be paid at the end of each quarter, following an appropriate inspection by the engineers of the Trans-Canada Highway of the Department of Public Works.
When will the federal government stop intruding in fields coming under provincial jurisdiction?
Interim Supply
The federal government is voting a sum to enable the province of Quebec to continue road construction in the Gaspe peninsula. As a result the inspectors of the federal government will check how the money will be used by the Quebec provincial government.
I would be pleased to know what the Quebec government thinks about that, since several provincial ministers object to joint plans.
But the federal government persists in increasing its intrusion as far as highways are concerned, a field coming under provincial jurisdiction.
I say, Mr. Chairman, it is a betrayal, on the part of the federal government, to try to invade a provincial jurisdictional field, namely that of the roads department.
Mr. Chairman, the province of Quebec wants a railway. The chamber of commerce of north Gaspe wishes to have this railway. The people in north Gaspe want this railway. Why does the federal government refuse to carry out the bill that was passed at the time we were in office? Why does the federal government refuse to comply with the request made by the chamber of commerce of north Gaspe, which really expresses the wish of the people of the Matapedia-Matane and north Gaspe areas?
At the present time, Mr. Chairman, we have only 11 per cent of all railway lines in Canada and the province of Quebec wants to increase its railway mileage.
Since when, Mr. Chairman, must growth come before the construction of the railway?
The minister said in his statement:
Should the region enjoy an economic growth that would warrant the construction of that railway, the project would of course be considered again.
Mr. Chairman, a railway must come before the growth of a region.
What would have happened if we had had to wait until the western provinces had developed to build a railway line from coast to coast?
Railroads must be the basis of economic development in an area, a province or a country. They must come before development. If the railroad in question is not built, the natural resources of that part of our province, the Gaspe area, will remain undeveloped.
Mr. Chairman, I am quite surprised to see the federal government further encroaching upon a field of provincial jurisdiction by asking its inspectors to check the work done by the Quebec department of highways.

Interim Supply
Mr. Chairman, is that the government's way of preparing for the by-election which will be held in the riding of Matane a few weeks hence?
Probably.

Mr. Chairman, why are the Gaspe chamber of commerce and the people of Quebec denied the right to carry out that legislation?
The minister knows the bill was approved. It was endorsed by all government members, including the former minister of transport and member for Laurier who has since been appointed Canada's high commissioner in London.
Seven minutes.

I will prove my co-operation in two minutes. I ask the minister, and I ask the government to construct this railway. It is very important to the economy of Gaspe, and it is very important to the economy of the province of Quebec. We are faced with unemployment. I say to this government, what have you in mind? Why do you postpone this project? The Gaspe chamber of commerce wants this project. We have a government which refuses to take its responsibility. We have a government which is unable to resolve the problem of unemployment and refuses to build this railway. We want to co-operate with the government. We are ready to adopt this interim supply resolution. We hope the Minister of Forestry will be back in the house within a few days because we have many questions to address to him. This is not the time for him to be on a holiday in Europe, when we are at work and when our constituents are asking us to work for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It was suggested to me last week, Mr. Chairman, that there were certain questions which hon. members wished to have answered with respect to my department prior to the usual time when the main estimates are introduced. I have waited until the end of this debate to see whether anything else might arise, but to my knowledge the only questions are the only ones asked last Tuesday in the debate which is recorded in Hansard for July 28. I have gone through the speeches and about 15-odd members contributed to the more than five hours spent on this department. I have gone through the record looking for questions, and I have found one or two with which I should deal.

The first speech was made by my predecessor, the hon. member for Perth. He dealt mainly with the health ministers' conference which had just concluded, and spent most of the remainder of his time making general remarks. He did indeed praise the fact that the Department of National Health and Welfare is now in a brand new building out at Tunney's pasture. He also made some reference-and I must confess I think he had a tongue in one or both cheeks when doing so -to the minister moving into the plushiest office in Ottawa. If members of the committee would permit me, I would like to thank my predecessor for the spending of $7 million on that building, and to thank him for having laid out this very magnificent 35 foot ministerial office. Indeed it is far more than such a modest person as I would arrange for myself, but I am very grateful for the foresight of my hon. friend.
I think the minister would admit I did let her know I was only jealous.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I would be very happy to invite my hon. friend out for a cup of tea and to walk with me around the balustrade overlooking the Gatineau hills and the beautiful river, and perhaps the two of us can find together the peace which he referred to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And how about
