speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, I would be very happy to take with me my predecessor's predecessor, who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I am afraid he would be a little troubling influence intervening between my predecessor and myself.
I would be an influence for good.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Subsequent to the hon. member for Perth speaking, there was a most interesting speech by the hon. member for Waterloo North which chiefly commended my department for its record with respect to the setting up of the parliamentary committee on pesticides, and commended the second report of that committee working under its very able chairman, the hon. member for Halton. His comments were very useful but he did not ask any questions at that point. Later he dealt at some length with a matter which is close to his heart, the fitness and amateur sports program, and I am very grateful for the congratulations he showered upon my department in that respect. He also dealt with the construction of facilities, which

had been dealt with a number of times previously in speeches, but he did not make any inquiries at that time.
The hon. member for Saskatoon, obviously a very gifted new member, made a speech which received commendation, and properly so, from many hon. members. It was a truly memorable maiden speech, and dealt with a subject with which she is well suited to deal as a psychiatrist. It is absolutely clear that she knows at first hand the problems of mental health. She did not pose any questions to the minister, and while much of what she dealt with falls within provincial responsibility, certainly the general principles to which she subscribed are supported by Mr. Justice Hall and his commissioners and have been subscribed to by the Department of National Health and Welfare for some considerable time.
Subsequently the hon. member for Simcoe East dealt with a subject which is often mentioned in the house, and on which he has repeatedly asked questions on orders of the day, namely the anti-cigarette smoking campaign of the department. He was good enough to compliment me for having stopped smoking and for the example which that gave to young people. He also complimented the department on the booklet of statistics it issued regarding fatalities and illnesses arising from cigarette smoking. He did ask a question or two about cigarette advertising and cigarette vending, both of which had been answered on orders of the day a month or so previously.
He also made a suggestion which I cannot really consider very seriously, that perhaps the government would like to set up a medical university in his riding. If he is serious about this I would be happy to discuss it with him, but I am sure he would appreciate that the federal government does not set up universities as such. This is a matter within the very jealously guarded prerogatives of the provinces.
The hon. member for London dealt lightly with assistance programs and did not ask any questions.
The hon. member for Springfield, who was a social worker and has considerable background in that work, dealt with the welfare side of my department. He dealt at some length with sheltered workshops and made a most interesting and helpful speech, but did not ask any questions. He also dealt with the conference on the family, which Their Excellencies the Governor General and Madame Vanier sponsored recently in Ottawa, and 20220-4081
Interim Supply
with the very useful things which it is hoped will arise from that.
The hon. member also raised several matters regarding Indian health and the provinces. This is very topical, since today we notice in the press that as a result of the meeting of the provincial premiers there is to be some further discussion among them regarding their adoption of responsibility for Indian health.
The hon. member for Wellington-Huron made a brief speech on smoking, without posing any questions. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin also spoke very briefly about the question of Indian hospitals.
The hon. member for Regina City dealt with the fitness program and commended me for the new appointments I made in January to the fitness and amateur sports advisory body. He also dealt at length with the possibility of obtaining grants for the soaring association of Canada, something in which he is much interested.
The hon. member for Grenville-Dundas accepted compliments on her approaching marriage and made a most interesting and able general speech regarding the department for which she had formerly the honour to be the parliamentary secretary. She concluded with the request that the government might consider implementation of one of the Hall commission recommendations, namely to undertake fluoridation wherever possible under its jurisdiction. I am sure the hon. member is aware that my parliamentary secretary earlier this session made a pronouncement on fluoridation on behalf of the department.
Then there was a request by the hon. member for Kootenay West that I and other lady members join together to see action was taken to let the female secretarial staff off early, because the temperature was 95 and the humidity 98. It seemed to me that the hon. member was at that point, although truly concerned as always with the well-being of any young ladies, mainly concerned with the well-being of the committee and hopeful he might alleviate a very threatening atmosphere which appeared to be developing at that time.
In all the five hours and 15 speeches there was one topic of some considerable weight raised by two hon. members, and I am glad to see one of them in the committee and interested enough to be here to hear the answer. The hon. member for Northwest Territories discussed a number of things, but principally he spoke of the question of the

Interim Supply
Charles Camsell hospital, which I had announced would be rebuilt in Edmonton. I am sure he has not had an opportunity to discuss this with his colleague, the former speaker of the house, who represents Edmonton West, or with any other Edmonton member, as I am certain the contents of his speech would not have received much agreement from them. The burden of his speech, which was supported by the hon. member for Athabasca later, was that the Charles Camsell hospital, a ramshackle collection of buildings in the city of Edmonton, put together and utilized at the moment for the special purposes of Indian and Eskimo health, should not be rebuilt.
It was pointed out that the Glassco commission on reorganization of the government, which sat for some time, had made an express comment regarding this hospital and a specific recommendation against rebuilding it. My hon. friend from the Northwest Territories suggested that the Eskimos and Indians in his area and contiguous areas might be better served by the construction of smaller hospitals in the territory, closer to the homes of the individuals. He expressed himself in favour of a policy of integration as opposed to a policy of segregation. I must say I agree with that general statement of policy. I am not in favour of segregation whether it be on the basis of background, colour or sex, and I believe all members of this committee are agreed that under successive governments Canada has for a number of years been moving toward the integration of our native people with those who arrived at a later date.
However the Charles Camsell hospital is a rather specialized matter. May I say that I was not aware, earlier in the day, that this debate would be closing this evening. Accordingly I shall have to speak from memory; I shall be in a position to deal with the subject at much greater length when my estimates are under consideration. This hospital, as has been said, is physically a collection of dilapidated buildings. I went to see it and I was shocked that any government would offer hospital services in such buildings. The maternity room was about 10 feet by 6 feet and had attached to it one bathroom in which the garbage can was kept. I saw babies from all over the territories, from all over Alberta, from the northern part of British Columbia and from the northern part of Saskatchewan brought in to the hospital, and all were kept in large wards without segregation. I looked at the charts over the beds and found that there was not one disease

diagnosed, but half a dozen. I asked about this, and I was told it was the regular practice-all the children were put in wards, together, so that they had an opportunity to catch other childhood diseases and acquire immunity. Incidentally this is something a mother often does when she has more than one child, in order to get them out of this particular stage. Many childhood diseases are not very serious when they are contracted at an early age.
The standard of care at the hospital was incredibly high. Doctors and nurses have come from all over the world to work there. Every facility is available in this scattered conglomeration of buildings. Facilities for operations are extremely poor, but they exist. Medical teams from the university come to the hospital and through this device Indian and Eskimo patients have available to them the best medical skills in our country. In the hospital I saw row upon row of Eskimo babies suffering from such things as congenital hips. These babies have been brought from their homes, and in order that they may recover it is necessary for them to stay for years in the hospital, sometimes from the time they are only two or three months old. I saw babies with tuberculosis who also may have to spend years under treatment. The Indians and the Eskimos, in particular the women, are famous among all people for the tremendous love and attention they show to their young ones, and to the young ones generally of the communities in which they live. Yet nothing can surpass the love and affection which is showered upon these babies so far from their own homes. The Indians and Eskimos to whom I spoke-and they were not many, since very few of them speak English and I do not have any of the native languages-pointed out to me the kind of facilities they have, the food, clothing and care they received. They told me they were homesick. This is something to which the hon. member drew the attention of the committee.
It happens to be a fact that my department, the Department of National Defence and, in some respects, the department of northern affairs are faced with an almost impossible task in trying to secure and keep first class medical people and para-medical people for service in the very far north. It is for this reason that the Charles Camsell hospital, which provides a whole range of services, is built in Edmonton. That is as far as we can go if we are to get the kind of personnel necessary in order to serve these people

properly. The opinion was expressed in the Glassco report that this hospital should be built on the university grounds, possibly as a wing of the existing hospital. It was not known by the members of the commission when preparing their report that the University of Alberta and the government of Alberta would not permit this, had decided that its hospital was already sufficiently large and that no room would be made available for any further extensions for any purpose. I would point out that at one point this project had been approved by my predecessor as the hon. gentleman will agree. Then on December 20, 1962, it was cancelled-I know the date because it happens to be my birthday and I had hoped to be able to make an announcement by December 20 of last year reversing that decision.
It is of course expensive to build such a hospital. It is difficult to justify putting it up for a class of people, and I do not like the idea any more than the hon. gentleman does. The responsibility of my department at the moment is to provide, as close as possible to their homes, the best medical facilities we can for the people who are the least civilized of our population-those who have the least money, the fewest facilities and the most restricted possibilities.
The hon. gentleman was generous enough to say in his speech that he was aware of the kind of money being spent by my department to fly out of the north anyone from children to old people, regardless of what was ailing them, in order that they might receive the best hospital care. We hope, and I am very proud of this as the minister responsible, that we can improve the standard of care by rebuilding the Camsell hospital. If the hon. gentleman would speak with his colleague the former Speaker, who is sitting beside him and who represents Edmonton West where the new hospital is to be built he will realize I think from that conversation the kind of devotion to their patients which is shown by the doctors and nurses and by the para-medical personnel who work there. I was driven to visit this particular hospital by their repeated pleas, and when I got there I felt as though a lot of puppies were following me around, they were so terribly anxious that their patients should have the facilities which they thought they were entitled to-not that there should be marble halls or a fancy public institution to which the local member could point with pride, but so that there would be cleanliness, space, and an opportunity for good health care.
Interim Supply
This is the reason why the department, taking well into consideration the recommendation of the Glassco commission report, which was based upon an erroneous impression, taking into consideration the possibility of further opening up the north by providing improved hospital facilities for Indians and Eskimos there, decided that notwithstanding the fact that it would be more appropriate to integrate, because of the history of absolute inability to obtain personnel and facilities so far above the tree line, the best thing which could be done was to proceed immediately to the reconstruction of this hospital.

Would the hon. lady permit a short question? Is she aware of the fact that the distant early warning line which spans the high Arctic hundreds of miles further north than the place I was suggesting as the site of a new hospital, has always been supplied with medical staff, and this was done by paying them $18,000 a year and everything found. I suggest the basic reason why the department is unable to recruit staff, if this is so, is that they are offering wages which are completely inadequate in the circumstances, so they are unlikely to get the services of anyone unless he is either desperate for experience or has something to run away from. I wonder whether the hon. lady has looked into this aspect of the situation when she says that medical staff refuse to go into the Canadian Arctic.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be happy to pay them the salary members of parliament are paid, or much more than that. I am not certain of the D.E.W. line situation but I assume that the hospitals there are staffed by the military.
Perhaps I should tell the committee of the situation in Churchill. The hon. member for Churchill might be able to hear this out. As hon. members know, recently the Department of National Defence closed down its facilities there and left a hospital. There was some considerable discussion as to whether the Department of National Defence should for a while operate this facility until Manitoba might take it over. After long discussions Manitoba decided to take it over as of August 1. Manitoba has been unable to find medical personnel who will go to Churchill, and accordingly has besought the federal government to keep its military medical personnel there, even such people as stretcher bearers, interns, doctors and nurses-almost all the personnel-until such time as they are able to improve this situation. I am not certain what

Interim Supply
the salary is, but I last heard that over $20,000 was being offered by the province of Manitoba to personnel-with no takers.
As my hon. friend will have noticed if he has been to the Charles Camsell hospital, as he says he has, many of its doctors were not trained in Canada; many of them have come here from different parts of Europe and Asia and the salaries they are receiving are perhaps much in excess of what they would be receiving elsewhere. But unhappily many of them work for a couple of years, get their qualifications and then leave. This has been a difficulty all along with the northern health service. I hope this explanation with regard to the chief question, and the only one which it seemed to me was asked for the purpose of getting information, will sufficiently satisfy my hon. friend and the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I just wanted to ask the Minister of Transport a couple of questions in connection with the Ste Anne des Monts railway. I heard the minister's comment that the translators encountered some difficulty with the statement. There are a couple of points I wanted to get clear in my mind. Is the legislation completely dead now? That is the first question.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I had better dispose of that question right away. I am not a lawyer, and the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition said I did not understand the act, and I just do not think it would be wise for me to attempt a technical explanation here. All I can say is that it is not the intention of the government, at the present time, to go on with the building of that railway.
I am glad the minister is in what he described earlier as one of his simple, artless moods.
I did not say "artless".

I am sure the minister has reviewed the evidence that was presented to the railway committee. Has he considered that anyone, either civil servants or politicians, might be liable for perjury charges, in view of the kind of evidence that was given in support of the building of this railway that now the government has decided should not be built?

Mr. Chairman, not being in the journalistic business but being at the present time Minister of Transport, I have not felt it necessary, being fully occupied with the duties of Minister of Transport, to consider whether or not anyone has committed

perjury; nor do I think it is appropriate to the functions of the head of a department which one of my predecessors has described as being too big for one man anyway, to go around looking for things to do in other people's fields. I will leave that problem to the hon. member for Port Arthur.

I am glad the minister is carrying on in this simple way today. I would hate him to think that I have not beside my bed that book he edited regarding Mackenzie King's diary, and I can never forget what a journalist he is, and an editor, too. With regard to the question of-

When do you get time to
sleep?
Well, one of my bedtime stories is the Minister of Transport's presentation of a hagiography of one of the great leaders of our nation.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman-
I have the floor.
I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister is rising on a question of privilege.

My question of privilege is certainly on the same level as questions of privilege put forward during the present session. It is that I wish to say that work was written when I was unfortunately unemployed. I am unemployed no longer.
I am glad the minister considers being in the opposition as being unemployed.

I assumed that was why the
hon. gentleman had another full time job.

I wanted to ask the minister what justification he is putting forward for the unilateral deal that seems to have been made with the Quebec government in this particular case, under no general program of any kind, unless it is as a sop or some kind of recognition after the event and trying to do something with a bad bill. I am not putting this question in direct terms; I am loading it. I would like to know the answer, because this matter bothers me very much. I am concerned about what has followed what I thought was a hopeless bill when it was brought in. The minister and his friends voted for it, and when they came into power I suppose the advice of the C.N.R. officials

finally got through to them, that this was uneconomical, that it was a real boondoggle, and so they stopped it.
But out of this has come, as far as I can see, a one-shot, unique kind of arrangement with the particular region, as compensation. It seems to me the minister should indicate whether other parts of the country can figure on this kind of arrangement if they have transportation facilities that cannot be improved by a railway, or are they going to be in the position of some of the western parts of the country and lose the railways they now have?
Is this a general principle that will be applied to other areas? Is the attitude the government is taking toward Gaspe to be the future policy, or are we to consider it, as the minister put it so simply and so artlessly- this is the way I took it, from his simple and artless approach-"Ha, ha, ha. You fellows thought you were going to buy votes in Gaspe, and now we are outbuying you with a slicker deal".

As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am a simple person. I did not say I was artless; I said I was a straightforward person. I try not to load my questions, and I am not going to try to load my answers. But this parliament did decide, with the hon. gentleman dissenting, that $16 million might be spent on improving transportation in this area. When we came into office and examined the information that was available to us, we thought that $16 million could be better applied in improving the transportation in the Gaspe area in the other way I described this afternoon, rather than in building a railway. For that reason-we did not do anything unilateral-we made an agreement with the government of Quebec to spend $13 million on the highway because we thought that was the best way to improve the transportation in that area.
We were told that the government of Quebec-which has a timetable for all its highways all over the province-could not get at this project for a number of years and it could be greatly speeded up if we contributed, in exactly the same way as the Atlantic development board the other day earmarked $10 million of its funds for the improvement of trunk roads in the Atlantic provinces, namely to try to speed up the development of transportation facilities in those areas which the the MacPherson commission said were in need of special help in regard to their transportation facilities. I would like to think that if there are railways that are performing
Interim Supply
a function rather inefficiently and are costing the treasury a lot of money, there would not be too much objection to closing the railway and putting something else in its place. I hope the government would have the common sense to do this, particularly if it would save the treasury money in the long run. It seemed to me this was the sensible way of dealing with this problem, and I hope to be able to deal sensibly with a great many other problems in respect of transportation in this country.

I should like to ask one final question. Will the vote on this particular item be the kind that will be brought in regularly every year under the minister's estimates in view of what he has said about the staging of this item? In other words, will there be a specific item devoted to this which we will be able to speak to during our consideration of the estimates, and will this be a continuing item over a number of years?

Quite frankly, sir, I have not had the time to discuss that matter with my colleagues on the treasury board, and until I do it would be wrong for me to answer. This item is not intended to be paid for out of the general vote of the department. There certainly will be a specific vote in respect of this project. The hon. gentleman said that was his last question.
I should like to make sure I understand the situation. Are you giving us assurance that there will be an opportunity, for those of us who wish to do so, to vote against this item?
Of course there will be an opportunity for hon. members to vote against this item if they wish to do so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to say a few words in this debate in reply to the very polite questions that have been asked by members on the other side concerning matters pertaining to the departments of agriculture and forestry. I realize that most of the questions are related to the Department of Forestry and have been directed in greater detail toward the ARDA program.
I suppose one reason that the agricultural department has been spared somewhat from questioning is due to the fact that consideration of the agriculture estimates concluded on July 10, after some five full days of debate. I suppose it is reasonable to assume that most of the questions concerning the Department of Agriculture were answered at that time.

Interim Supply
I presume also that the notably improved relations in this chamber are the result of the summit conference which has taken place, and I should think that more summit conferences would be helpful.
I think one of the main questions asked by the opposition has related to the presence of the Minister of Forestry in the house. I have a short statement which indicates the Minister of Forestry is attending an international conference in Italy at the invitation of Hon. Mario Ferrari-Aggradi, the minister of agriculture and forestry of Italy. He is on a study tour of the integrated development in the mountainous territory of Italy. In addition he is going to attend a number of top level meetings with the prominent officials of the department of agriculture of Italy concerning the export of Canadian wood products to Italy. In addition there will be a number of meetings held with prominent officials of FAO concerning policies of that country and other countries attending the conference relating to rural development and forestry. I feel quite justified in assuring the committee that while the Minister of Forestry is in Italy at this particular time he is on Canadian business at all times.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The other matter that has been given some prominence relates to the ARDA program. I think when the minister was here in the house he paid justifiable tribute to the former minister of agriculture and the government for having instituted this program in 1961 and for the steps forward that were taken by that government in connection with the ARDA program.
We of course all remember that this was a three year experiment, that some $50 million was allocated to this particular program, and that the contracts with the provinces are to expire in 1965. The Minister of Forestry, under whose direction the ARDA program has been placed, has undertaken to visit all the provinces in Canada, to assess the problems of those provinces and discuss them with the provincial authorities. He intends to return and prepare a program which will encompass the over-all needs of the provinces as they vary from one to another. He proposes to devise a program to enter into new contracts which will be necessary in 1965.
I think it is fair to add that in addition to the excellent work that was carried out by the former administration, the ARDA program has been pushed forward and is being extended by the present administration.

Some mention was made of the dutch elm disease by the hon. member for Prince Ed-ward-Lennox. This situation is of continuing concern to the Minister of Forestry, and to myself in particular, because I do not think there is another area in Canada where elm trees are affected more than in my riding, the county of Peel, and where the loss has caused more grave concern. This type of work being done by the Minister of Forestry is being felt everywhere. There is a program in progress in respect of research to meet the needs of changing conditions in forestry at all times.
Some mention has been made of the feed grain policy of this government, which of course now comes under the authority of the Minister of Forestry. Of course we are aware of the changes made as of October last year as a result of which this government undertook to provide freight assistance in respect of grains moving to eastern Canada for feed purposes. In addition the government undertook to pay storage on all these feed grains, because there was a real problem resulting in the fluctuating of the price to eastern users. I think it is probably fair to observe that the price of feed grains has been more or less stabilized during the past few months because there is continuity of supply. Of course it will be of interest to hon. members to know that this matter has been referred to the committee on colonization and agriculture for further study and will be given further attention as required.
Some mention has been made of credit facilities for farmers. We are aware of the improvements which have been instituted in recent months and of some of the anticipated measures which will assist farmers in arranging credit in a more convenient way.
I do not propose to delay this debate in any way, Mr. Chairman, but I felt some of the questions that were asked by members on the other side were worthy of courteous replies. I will be happy to sit down now, and if there are any additional questions I will be pleased to answer them to the best of my ability.

Mr. Chairman, before the end of this debate, I would like to make some remarks which I feel are necessary.
Since yesterday, we have noted a drastic change of attitude among the members of the official opposition as well as the ministers.
Much importance has been attached during the past two days to the 200 questions asked by the official opposition as a proof that the said official opposition did not abdicate its responsibilities in this house and that it

would succeed in compelling the ministers to speak and to answer the questions asked.
A moment ago the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) analysed several speeches dealing with her department and only answered a few questions. Therefore, she is not the one who will answer all the questions concerning her department.
Many suggestions were made this afternoon. One might have thought, for instance, that the Conservatives discovered the Gaspe peninsula only a few months before the 1963 election.
After hearing the many suggestions made over the past week during the debate on interim supply, one is inclined to forget that only one year and a few months have elapsed since the Conservatives were defeated. Everything has to be done over again and all kinds of suggestions have been made in the last ten or 12 days.
Up to a year and a few months ago, the Conservatives had been responsible for the administration of the country for six years.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) rose three times in the course of this debate to speak about the serious problems facing Quebec agriculture; however, official statistics show that in 1957 farm revenues in the province of Quebec totalled $185 million and dropped to $179 million in 1962.
Mr. Chairman, we are wondering whether yesterday's summit conference had really anything to do with the change of heart which we have seen this afternoon regarding the end of this filibuster, if I may call it that, or whether we have to go back a few weeks when we read in the press that the Conservatives were demanding that the government withdraw its flag resolution, even threatening, according to certain statements made in Toronto or elsewhere by their leader, to extend the debate for as long as possible before giving final approval to this flag resolution. It lasted what it lasted. For almost a week, we heard about flags. After that, some thought they had found a way to postpone the debate on the flag by threatening the party in office to keep the debate on interim supply going; for a week, they really went in for what can be called a filibuster. Even if they claimed that it was a matter of 200 odd questions put to various ministers, I think that instead they made general remarks on the future policy of the Conservative party which sits in the house today.
However, at the end of last week newspapers which are considered very sym-
Interim Supply
pathetic toward the official opposition, found such tactics unreasonable and useless in the present situation.
The Globe and Mail said that it was inadmissible strategy, when so many economic problems went begging for a solution, to drag on a debate only to prevent a decision from being taken on the matter of national symbols and emblems.
For fear of losing face somewhere along the line, it was agreed to hold a summit conference. As the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Caouette) stated this afternoon, in view of the rights of parliament and of its members, which rights are sacred as the Leader of the Opposition often said, this conference which, according to this morning's newspapers, lasted 25 minutes is a complete contempt and denial of the rights of members of third parties who still represent over 25 per cent of Canadian voters in this house.
Mr. Chairman, I do not feel that the speeches made by various ministers since yesterday afternoon constitute a reply to the 200-odd questions which were mentioned. First, we heard the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) overwhelm with congratulations the Conservative members who had made suggestions concerning the improvement of his department. He named them all probably for the purpose of putting their names in Hansard so that the record would show the negligible role played by the third parties during the important debate on interim supply. But as a large improvement, he has not yet found the manner in which to tell us what his department will do to stop many Canadian citizens from expatriating themselves, from emigrating to other countries because they are compelled at present to turn to our neighbours to earn a living. As a matter of fact, in 1962, more than 45,000 Canadians asked for visas to go to work permanently for our neighbours to the south. Forty five thousand. And we boast of having invited and received on our territory, under the Immigration Act, approximately a hundred thousand immigrants.
Of course, the minister indicated that immigration would become more and more effective and more selective, in order to meet more adequately the needs of our country for skilled men and technicians.
He mentioned, among other things, Algerian immigrants who, under an agreement reached with the Quebec provincial government, will come and show the Canadians of that province how to farm. They are probably used to farm

Interim Supply
in the African desert, but they will come and show us how we ought to farm in the province of Quebec.
The difference, Mr. Chairman, is that those future immigrants who will join us here in Canada, will not lack credit to allow them to buy two or three farms, under the ARDA program applied in the province of Quebec, where families and generations succeeded one another, earning an honourable but hard living on family farms. Today these same farmers cannot get from the federal Farm Credit Corporation enough credit to be able to improve their means of production.
It is the same as the argument which we often heard expounded by the minister in other parts of the country, when he stated in Toronto, about two months ago: What we lack in Canada is a greater population.
That is why his department planned to facilitate immigration to Canada. We needed consumers, he said.
But I have not much faith in this theory because, to my mind, when consumers are brought in we also bring in mouths-yes mouths-and arms to produce things.
Whenever somebody is invited to come as a consumer he is also asked to become a producer.
If you have ten or 12 lame people who go oil together on a pilgrimage, whether they start one after another or all together, I do not think there will be a great difference with regard to their lameness; they will limp along to the end of the pilgrimage.
The same is true in respect of agricultural problems in eastern Canada. All surveys prove that millions of dollars were paid to western producers under various pieces of legislation.
For a long time the farming industry has been considered solely on the basis of Canadian wheat in this house. In the two years I have been sitting in the house, every time we discuss our farming industry, for days on end the problems of wheat and cattle breeding in western Canada and of western cattle auctions are mentioned. On the other hand, we did not often hear about the farming problems of Quebec. That is probably the reason why under the previous administration the eastern farmers' income constantly fell off whereas in western Canada the producers' income showed an increase of over $400 million during the same period.
We are used to have a policy along this line. What is black in Vancouver is white in Halifax. We have a policy for one part of the country, and another one for the other.

We are spending funds in some areas of the country in the form of grants, subsidies and farm assistance, or else, of crop insurance. Therefore, we are participating jointly with provincial governments, which have established such programs, and the ultimate result is that the implementation of these various acts providing assistance, after a few years, as revealed by the report of the royal commission on the administration of prairie farm assistance, of June 10-
Shame.

So it would seem. Under different acts jointly implemented by the provinces and the federal government, in some provinces, it is discovered, that although in 1962 the western farmers were supposed to have had an increase in revenue of $400 million, thanks especially to an abundant wheat crop in that year-it is precisely during that year 1962 that some things happened in the Department of Agriculture, and more particularly in the prairie farm assistance board -not too many comments were heard on this subject.
I went over this particular report twice. I may assure you it reveals some things which, in my opinion, eastern Canada farmers ought to be made aware. And we shall see who, in certain quarters, got the most from the farm policy of the federal government, and why such policy is so much to the disadvantage of some farming groups in other parts of the country.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh), who was quite interested in seeing the cheques sent on the date prescribed by the act, said that if farmers were entitled to allowances the cheques should be sent at the latest in December of the same year. The cheques were sent at the end of March, due to certain influence-this is what the report of this commission seems to say.
Last week and even this week, attempts were made to deny the value of this report. May I quote only a few paragraphs in the appendix of this report on page 51. When I read the evidence supplied by farmers directly interested in the matter, I see something significant in the way this legislation is applied.
I admit that the commissioner was right not to name the farmers concerned, but he added that those who would like to obtain further details might get them through the verbatim report. However, here they were known as members. An investigation was

made among 103 farmers in a single district of Saskatchewan.
Some significant facts were brought to light:
Farmer No. 2-500 bushels of old wheat were mistakenly carried over in his 1962 reports. His output for 1962 was incorrectly measured. It should have been 3,313 bushels instead of the 2,005 he reported; that would have increased his yield from 8.9 to 14.5 bushels per acre.
That would have made a very big difference in the P.F.A.A. subsidy-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to interrupt him to raise a point affecting the business of the committee which I believe is of interest to all hon. members. In view of the remarks made in the committee earlier this afternoon, I should like to ask the committee's permission to withdraw the resolution for two months' interim supply and to substitute for it a resolution for three months' interim supply. The effect of this, if it is done in the next moment or two, will be that the resolution for three months' interim supply will be printed in Hansard and will be before the committee. Then, hon. members will know exactly what items are in that resolution. If we can deal with it in all stages tonight, that would be fine, but if not this procedure would be to the advantage of all hon. members.

Agreed.
{Translation]

Mr. Chairman, about the point raised by the President of the Privy Council, there is no doubt that if such a proposal were adopted, it would have great significance.
If we are asked to vote interim supply for three months instead of two, what does it mean? That it is expected that the recess will start soon and that we could be asked to study an interim budget when the house comes back in the fall.
How can we decide today without any news about the meeting of the party leaders which is taking place? If they do not reach an understanding, are we going to sit until the end of September? We do not object to that, mind you. In such a case, it is useless to vote three months' interim supply.
If there is an agreement, and, as hon. members must meet their electors during the intersession, and as it would not be proper to start with interim supply immediately after the intersession, then it would be proper to vote three months' interim supply instead of
Interim Supply
two months. But we have no report as yet on this party leaders' meeting.
The Prime Minister said publicly yesterday that that meeting with the five party leaders would take place yesterday afternoon. It has not taken place but there have been secret caucuses between the leader of the party in office and the Leader of the Opposition, no attention being given the splinter parties, which should have had something to say.
They have been openly ignored. Arrangements were made yesterday between 4 and 4.30 p.m. between the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition. Following those arrangements, it has been noted that since last evening the ministers one after the other have been nicely and politely answering the questions of the Conservative members, something they refused to do previously.
What agreement has been reached in secret by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister? Why has the Prime Minister not kept his promise to convene a meeting of the five party leaders? Only two were called to that meeting.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It being six o'clock- [Text]
Order; shall I call it six o'clock?
No, no.

Mr. Chairman, we are ready to call it six o'clock unless we are given a report on the discussions which took place between the leaders of the five parties. If we do not get any information about that meeting, I fail to see what good it would do to vote supply for three months instead of two but, on the other hand, if there is an understanding-we are told that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) had every intention not to give in and to put off the flag debate until the fall, without any time limit-then we are not interested in seeing that debate postponed until the fall. Moreover, I know that the members of the Liberal party feel the same way and that they are not interested in having it put off until the fall without any time limit, because they know beforehand that it would kill the bill.
Under these conditions, it is better to declare that it is six o'clock, since we do not know where we stand. However, if a cabinet member is ready to give us a report on those discussions, we would be prepared to continue the debate and to reach an agreement

Business of the House
very soon, but if they will not let us have a report, we will point out immediately that it is six o'clock.
Since I had the floor, Mr. Chairman, I believe it is in order that I should be the one to ask you to declare that it is six o'clock.

May I point out that the offer I made to the committee, or the proposal I put before the committee, was not contingent upon information from any of the leaders whatever. It was put forward by me on the strength of the remarks made publicly in the committee this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the question. This suggestion was made by the leader of the official opposition, and we wish to stress that we do not care too much for any secret meetings between the leaders of the two main parties, because the other parties have been neglected since yesterday, although they had been told that their views would be sought.
That is why we prefer to call it six o'clock since they refuse to give us any information.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind you that it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I call it six o'clock?

Carried.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the acting house leader would confer with the hon. member for Lapointe and let us know what the business will be for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As soon as we conclude the discussion on interim supply, which I assume will take very little time tomorrow, we will go on with the second reading of Bill No. C-111, to provide for the revision of certain fiscal arrangements, and at the conclusion of that we will take up the flag debate.
Since our requests-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It being six o'clock this house stands adjourned until two o'clock tomorrow afternoon.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, August 6, 1964
